description: Dialogue imported verbatim from source-tweets, plus the preserved bakery queue conversation. No quest, reward, or game-state effects are implied.

dialogues.title: Imagine telling a guy in 1900 that a hundred years in the future, you can fly...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Imagine telling a guy in 1900 that a hundred years in the future, you can fly across the country in five hours for the price of 4 ham sandwiches.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Is it dangerous? No, it is the safest form of transport.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: People must love it! No, it is so commonplace that people whine endlessly.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Air travel is incredible. It is probably the best example of a well-regulated highly competitive market economy creating an almost at-cost public utility, ceding oodles and oodles of surplus value to the consumer.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Sometimes I think of this in the context of what people might complain about a few hundred years from now.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: My immortality drugs are giving me a headache. [rolls eyes]

dialogues.title: I was talking with my Uber driver...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I was talking with my Uber driver...

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I'm paying $47.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: He's getting paid $10.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: I don't think this can last.

dialogues.title: I have always dismissed birdwatching as a hobby, but now I'm in my early 30s ...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I have always dismissed birdwatching as a hobby, but now I'm in my early 30s on an 8am walk in the park...

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: And I saw a tiny creature with magnificent blue feathers on the path ahead of me, so bright and azure that I instinctively took out my camera for a photo.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Maybe I get it now.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: In the 1800s, people went to the forest to painstakingly collect and catalogue every possible beetle.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: In 2025, you go to the park to photograph and identify every bird.

dialogues.title: If you know a lot about software, then you will recognize how poorly most of ...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: If you know a lot about software, then you will recognize how poorly most of it is built.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: But it's not poor by happenstance, it is poor by choice. And the choice of the software publisher is that they don't care about you.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: This is just so sad.

dialogues.title: I think Curtis Yarvin's work is largely not very good. It's not very rigorous...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I think Curtis Yarvin's work is largely not very good. It's not very rigorous and hand-waves way too many important arguments.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: But I get why it's popular -- it's the most visible, mainstreamed work that is truly reactionary against the present day.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: People sense that something is awry, so they read Yarvin. I get it.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Isn't that an indictment on the contemporary intellectual scene? If Yarvin's the best writer to advance your views, then what does that say about your views?

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: You'd expect much more skilled writers to show up and make these cases, but that whole scene is just paltry.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: I think Yarvin's prose is actually pretty bad, which I suppose makes it even more damning.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: I could complain at length about his prose, but I think the much more important issue is the content of his writing.

dialogues.title: My dad bought a book on Carl Jung from Amazon.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: My dad bought a book on Carl Jung from Amazon.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: He's a few pages in, telling me how bad it is.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: I look. The cover looks like Dall-E. The text formatting has messy white space. The introduction's third sentence is "Jung was not X, he was Y."

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: The entire book is ChatGPT generated!

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: Self-published, print-on-demand in 2026... What do we expect?

dialogues.title: I'm always stunned by this asymmetry:

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I'm always stunned by this asymmetry:

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Eating 400 calories is extremely easy, a snickers two-pack. Just a little snack.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Losing 400 calories requires a serious,  sweaty, half hour workout (or longer).

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Just existing for 4 hours also burns 400 calories.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Correct, but I cannot add another four hours to my day.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: If you want the flavor of chocolate but not the calories, maybe just put it in your mouth and then spit it out.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: I get it, but no.

dialogues.title: I bought a refill pack of my shower gel from Amazon. It runs a lot thinner th...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I bought a refill pack of my shower gel from Amazon. It runs a lot thinner than the original.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: So I checked my order: fulfilled by Amazon, supplied by third party. They literally watered it down. I am so tired of this.

dialogues.title: So I think Mayor Lurie's been doing a good job.

line-1.speaker: player
line-1.text: So I think Mayor Lurie's been doing a good job.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Yeah hundred percent except the speeding cameras. You hear about this shit?

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: No, all I know is that during Covid, SF dropped its traffic law enforcement to zero.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Well now they got these speeding cameras all over town and I'm getting all these tickets or whatever.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: Uh-huh.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: Yeah they added all these speed limits everywhere too it's bullshit man. Now everything's a 20 mile an hour zone and if I'm going 31 in a 20 I'm gonna get fined fifty fucking bucks? Fucking bullshit.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: Uh-huh yeah that's crazy. [internally: YES! YES! STRAIGHT INTO MY VEINS! AHHHH!]

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Yeah I got 7 of these damn things already.

line-9.speaker: player
line-9.text: Wow no way. [internally: I am so happy.]

dialogues.title: An interesting thing about tech vs. finance is how much cultural power founde...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: An interesting thing about tech vs. finance is how much cultural power founders have.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: You could pull $10M/year at Citadel or DE Shaw and ~nobody would know who you are.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Founders? You can pull zero revenue but post about the dream of greatness to achieve moderate celebrity status.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: There's something romantic here, come to think of it. Founders do not necessarily have to achieve the big numbers.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: They can still win respect just by trying their best and inspiring others. The courage of the man in the arena is to be admired.

dialogues.title: Sometimes I think about gun control: from about 2010 to 2015 it felt like thi...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Sometimes I think about gun control: from about 2010 to 2015 it felt like this was the dominant issue in US politics.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: And I wonder whether this was a mistake from the mainstream dems -- too contentious an issue with too little payoff.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: It was probably clear from the start that gun control proponents could never achieve a sufficient majority to enact real change.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Let alone the obvious practical impossibility of carrying out gun control in a country with several hundred million guns in circulation.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: At the same time, it alienated a ton of conservative voters and drove a deep demographic/ideological divide.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: It would've been possible to drive change on bipartisan issues that wouldn't have contributed to polarization.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: In retrospect, it all looks like a strategic misfire, an overextension and overspend of political capital on something that never carried true popular appeal.

dialogues.title: It's funny how dated ~2015 startup culture feels now. "We have beer on tap! W...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: It's funny how dated ~2015 startup culture feels now. "We have beer on tap! We're a fun company!"

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: Today there are no startups with beer on tap. To most young engineers, the idea of even drinking alcohol in general seems strange and suboptimal.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: I haven't seen a ping-pong table in an office in years.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: A lot of current startup culture is highly performative -- virtually none of the people who claim to work 996 actually do, most of the office bunk beds are never used, etc. But the culture is still a lot more ambitious and concrete than it was ten years ago.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: There was a lot of woo-ish bullshit in the early 2010s. Companies had ambitions to change the world, but with stuff like a Yoga-Centric Social Network or Cat-Sitting Apps.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: This crop of startups seems to have died out and been replaced with a much more hardcore and optimized views -- laser-focused on big TAMs, shifting economic value from labor to technology, and summoning the Machine God.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: It may feel like there's a lot of startup grift these days -- and there is -- but that's just because of the sheer size of the ecosystem now. Some of the froth bubbles over.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: But on a whole it feels far more serious, ambitious, and actually world-changing than when I arrived ten years ago. Silicon Valley is out of its teenage years and in adulthood now.

line-9.speaker: player
line-9.text: There's probably some extent to which this is a washing out of the "tech weirdo" culture, and a replacement by a more professionalized culture.

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: Tech today is no longer as Burning Man adjacent, fewer engineers are misfits elsewhere, and it's also less accessible to bootcamps and the like.

line-11.speaker: player
line-11.text: Product Managers today would've been Investment Bankers 15 years ago. It's like a game where the metagame has slowly become figured out, and what was once fringe is now mainstream.

dialogues.title: On the wealth tax: you should be *extremely worried* that California is runni...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: On the wealth tax: you should be *extremely worried* that California is running record budget deficits during the *good part* of the economic cycle.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: California has a massive spending problem. The state's public finances are being robbed.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: More taxes won't fix a bottomless pit.

dialogues.title: My wife said, Do you think moving back to California was a bad idea? Cause of...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: My wife said, Do you think moving back to California was a bad idea? Cause of the taxes and mismanagement and all.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: And so I said, California is a blessed land and I will fight tooth and nail for good policy on its soil.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: And she said, Fight? You mean tweet? Post all day?

dialogues.title: The "weed guy" as cultural archetype has completely disappeared.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: The "weed guy" as cultural archetype has completely disappeared.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: Musicians like Snoop Dogg or Wiz Khalifa who made it their whole personality are irrelevant now.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Legalization normalized it. There's no counterculture left in it, no edge, it's just dated.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Among movies, "stoner comedies" like Pineapple Express are completely obsolete.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: There's more to it! It used to be that this particular "weed guy" archetype selected for people who were a bit rebellious and therefore interesting.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: But now that the rebellious have moved elsewhere, the "weed guy" that's leftover is just tremendously boring.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: Because of course marijuana tends to slow people down, make them complacent, a little lazy -- boring.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: You may not even know any of these people, because they tend to just hang out by themselves, stoned, alone, at home. This is now an antimemetic personality.

dialogues.title: You can instantly drop off the hedonic-financial treadmill by changing your s...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: You can instantly drop off the hedonic-financial treadmill by changing your social context.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: In SF I spend tons of money on, and have impossibly high standards for, meals.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: When I'm with my parents, I eat boiled potatoes with salt.

dialogues.title: An airport is an interesting social environment in that it's basically totall...

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: An airport is an interesting social environment in that it's basically totally crime-free.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: Why is this?

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: Surveillance? The security check? A socioeconomic filter in having purchased a ticket?

line-8.speaker: player
line-8.text: "Why are there no pickpockets at an airport" sounds like a banal question, but I think there's some depth to it.

dialogues.title: The Epstein/Gates saga has a funny lesson for utilitarians.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: The Epstein/Gates saga has a funny lesson for utilitarians.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Gates has given more money to charity than anyone alive, and personally accounts for saving 80M+ lives.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Yet this has never done anything for him, or the perception of his ethics.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: The public hates him all the same.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: To the average news reader, his legacy right now looks to be "the guy who gave his wife an std from a prostitute and tried to surreptitiously sneak her the meds."

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: Make of this what you will.

dialogues.title: It's remarkable that GitHub Copilot blew its lead to a bunch of small startup...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: It's remarkable that GitHub Copilot blew its lead to a bunch of small startups. Should've been a slam-dunk.

dialogues.title: Despite the ubiquity of vomit bags in airplanes, I've never once seen them used.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Despite the ubiquity of vomit bags in airplanes, I've never once seen them used.

dialogues.title: One time I saw a Series B founder shoplift and that really told me everything...

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: One time I saw a Series B founder shoplift and that really told me everything about how his company would go.

dialogues.title: In the past year, I've been running into more and more people saying "{X} is ...

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: In the past year, I've been running into more and more people saying "{X} is my life's work".

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Maybe it's an early-30s thing, or maybe it's that everyone is trying to stake out some core areas of meaning before the AI wave washes over us.

dialogues.title: As we're living through exponential technological takeoff, it's more importan...

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: As we're living through exponential technological takeoff, it's more important than ever to journal and to write down one's impressions as time goes, because otherwise the incremental improvements make it so hard to pin down exactly how something was at a given point in time.

line-11.speaker: npc
line-11.text: I already regret not recording short YouTube videos of what it was like e.g. programming at the end of 2023 vs. 2024 vs. 2025. These are totally different experiences now.

dialogues.title: I had an interesting "gender is real and not just a construct" moment the oth...

line-14.speaker: npc
line-14.text: I had an interesting "gender is real and not just a construct" moment the other day.

line-15.speaker: npc
line-15.text: I had a female Uber driver late at night. And we ended up chatting about the "female driver" feature for female riders and how it was a huge change in terms of safety perception for women, and really popular.

line-16.speaker: npc
line-16.text: For me as a man, this hadn't occurred to me at all.

dialogues.title: Every day I have to log into like 50 different things and every single one of...

line-18.speaker: npc
line-18.text: Every day I have to log into like 50 different things and every single one of them wants me to enter a 2FA code and click a link in my email and ENOUGH.

line-20.speaker: npc
line-20.text: Let me have an API key and then interact with things programmatically.

line-21.speaker: npc
line-21.text: If I lose, let's say, 10 minutes a day on average to just logging into things, then that's what -- 3600 minutes a year?

dialogues.title: At this point, do YouTube/TikTok/etc. still do any meaningful copyright enfor...

line-24.speaker: npc
line-24.text: At this point, do YouTube/TikTok/etc. still do any meaningful copyright enforcement on audio tracks?

line-25.speaker: npc
line-25.text: I remember this being pretty tight in 2010, but it feels like this entire ship has sailed by now.

dialogues.title: "Culture as food" is an incredibly shallow view.

line-27.speaker: npc
line-27.text: "Culture as food" is an incredibly shallow view.

line-28.speaker: npc
line-28.text: You mention any country, culture, ethnic group, etc. and the default response is "Have you tried the [starch with meat]?"

line-29.speaker: player
line-29.text: Or, for example, there are lots of good reasons to be pro-immigration, but "so I can have more [foreign vegetable soup] at low prices" is not one of them.

line-30.speaker: npc
line-30.text: Cultures are more than just their culinary products, and reducing them to that feels deeply unsatisfying.

dialogues.title: The irony of "security questions" on any given online service is that they te...

line-32.speaker: npc
line-32.text: The irony of "security questions" on any given online service is that they tend to be pretty similar -- mother's maiden name, childhood best friend name -- which means that the more of them you use, the less secure they get.

line-33.speaker: player
line-33.text: Because surely one of these services will be breached at some point.

line-34.speaker: npc
line-34.text: My trash pickup service, which truly is not technically sophisticated, has made me set all these recovery questions, and I'm just thinking: surely these will wind up in public.

dialogues.title: I really wish that iCloud notes had a git-style version history.

line-36.speaker: npc
line-36.text: I really wish that iCloud notes had a git-style version history.

line-37.speaker: player
line-37.text: It would be so easy to do since it's all plaintext.

line-38.speaker: npc
line-38.text: I don't get why they haven't.

dialogues.title: Movies aren't doing super well these days, and I think a big part of the redu...

line-40.speaker: npc
line-40.text: Movies aren't doing super well these days, and I think a big part of the reduced appeal is that they struggle to capture the digital age.

line-41.speaker: player
line-41.text: Most movies are still set in a pre-tech world, one with libraries and phone calls and such.

line-42.speaker: npc
line-42.text: It's hard to make a good movie where the characters are mostly on their phones.

line-43.speaker: player
line-43.text: Any realistic romance movie nowadays would mostly be about people texting.

dialogues.title: When I was a child, I thought that landfills were terrible.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: When I was a child, I thought that landfills were terrible.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Just dumping everything in one spot seems so messy and contrary to the legibility and order that we think of as good.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: Not to mention the environment: isn't it bad just to put all the garbage in the ground?

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: In my childish mind, everything should have been cleanly sorted for recycling. It seemed so dumb to just dump it on one big pile on the ground.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Now it turns out that this is probably optimal.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: Right. We've learned that most "recycling" is a scam, where garbage gets sold and resold between recycling venues until finally it ends up with somebody who just dumps it into the Pacific ocean.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: On the other hand, putting stuff in a landfill is cheap and scalable.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: It's easy to fit a lot of stuff in a landfill, and ensure that it doesn't spread everywhere -- when you're done, you can cover it.

line-9.speaker: player
line-9.text: What's most interesting is that a landfill is fully recoverable.

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: When there's any kind of materials shortage, you can in fact just go to the landfill and start mining it, which has started happening over the last couple of years.

line-11.speaker: player
line-11.text: Enterprising governments/people are mining their landfills for rare earth metals, and it's working.

line-12.speaker: npc
line-12.text: Which really just makes the landfill a kind of a temporary deposit structure before eventually recycling or reusing those materials in a more efficient way.

line-14.speaker: npc
line-14.text: Maybe this is one of those "worse is better" cases.

dialogues.title: Unless we hit the software singularity, the way AI-enabled engineering is goi...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Unless we hit the software singularity, the way AI-enabled engineering is going to play out is something like this:

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: 1. Codebases are going to 10-100x in size and complexity, thanks to the AI's prolific ability to write code. Why? Most codebases are wildly under-built, with endless bugs to fix and backlogs of features to add.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: 2. The size/complexity expansion eventually hits some scaling limit in size/taste -- not for fault of the AI, but for fault of the engineer's ability to correctly specify *what they want* initially -- and then engineering skill + intuition matters again, just at a much larger scale of codebase/abstraction.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: 3. Right now is a weird spot in the engineering meta where people are having AI write 1x-size codebases and saying "Wow this is so easy, totally different skill set" but not realizing that most codebases are bad. 1x is not the benchmark for work completion: 10x is the benchmark now.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: 4. Gaining leverage is the story of software engineering over the last sixty years. I can write in Python in twenty minutes what would take me two weeks in pure C. AI adds a similar leverage multiplier.

dialogues.title: I moved to Silicon Valley when I was 23. Like many other people in my cohort,...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I moved to Silicon Valley when I was 23. Like many other people in my cohort, I helped out on some startups and got some equity.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I carefully thought about how much that equity might be worth one day. Maybe a million dollars? A life-changing amount of money for a 23-year-old.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Almost ten years later, some of this equity has appreciated a lot, but it's still not liquid.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Even if it were to be liquid soon, it's a far cry from what I imagined: at 33, and after nine years of inflation, a million dollars isn't a life-changing amount of money anymore.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: At 23, this money would've bought a lot of joy and opportunity -- but at 33, that time and situation has, to some extent, passed. They say that youth is wasted on the young and money is wasted on the old.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: Perhaps your time preference should be shorter if the assets are compounding on someone else's terms, and longer if they're compounding on your terms.

dialogues.title: 40 person line at Arsicault bakery at 10:40 on a Friday. All of these people ...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: 40 person line at Arsicault bakery at 10:40 on a Friday. All of these people are "working from home", I'm sure.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: Ha! Who are all these people in the gym with me at 2pm? Don't they have jobs?

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: I had a work meeting right next door!

dialogues.title: It is very sad that Spotify is fundamentally not an app for people who like m...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: It is very sad that Spotify is fundamentally not an app for people who like music.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Oftentimes I want to search through my Spotify library. It's like 10,000 songs and I want to grab all the ones that I added in the summer of 21.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Can't do that. Maybe I want to grab all the ones with samples from Michael Jackson. Can't do that. Maybe I want to grab all the ones with a particular lyric. Can't do that.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Maybe I want to find all the albums with red cover art. Or find all albums I liked that came out in 2020. Nope!

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: We have AI now. The search and ability to curate could be so good!

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: If I download all of my Spotify data, I can build all of the search myself. I'm just so disappointed that the Spotify team has never bothered enabling a better search.

dialogues.title: At dinner, I was made aware of an SF-based 22-year-old CEO whose "attention s...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: At dinner, I was made aware of an SF-based 22-year-old CEO whose "attention span is so cooked, when he has to review a legal document, someone on engineering has to vibe code him a video game that walks him through the legal language as a subway surfers adventure."

dialogues.title: At the start of this year I thought I was going to try to read two books a mo...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: At the start of this year I thought I was going to try to read two books a month.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I am now reading zero books for the rest of the year. Why?

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: AI is getting so much better that I have so much more leverage on my own time that it is becoming way too expensive to spend time on reading.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Projects that previously would have taken me 1,000 hours I can now do in 20.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Everything that I've ever dreamed of creating, writing, etc., that was previously out of reach, is suddenly within reach: just another 10 hours here, another 10 hours there, having and being able to use all of this AI leverage when other people aren't, feels like a huge advantage.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: That feels like the hottest possible iron that must be struck immediately.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: I've always been a standard-issue Silicon Valley nerd who's sometimes going to stay in and write software instead of going out, but now I'm feeling this stronger than ever before.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: The opportunity cost on my time has risen wildly and, funnily enough, this totally locks in my behavior.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: Instead of relaxing more, doing the same amount of work, and having more free time, I am busier than ever before.

line-10.speaker: player
line-10.text: Jevons Paradox is very, very real.

dialogues.title: I was reading about UChicago. In 1929, the 30-year-old dean of Yale Law Schoo...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I was reading about UChicago. In 1929, the 30-year-old dean of Yale Law School, Robert Maynard Hutchins, became president.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Can you imagine a 30-year-old being dean of Yale Law School today? Totally impossible.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: Our society of the young and dynamic has become a society of the old.

dialogues.title: Before the ~1980s, there was no portable music player. You'd go running, rowi...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Before the ~1980s, there was no portable music player. You'd go running, rowing, cycling, whatever, for hours on end, in total silence, no sound other than your own thoughts. How did they do it?

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: We will never know.

dialogues.title: I frequently ask engineering candidates what the difference between a git reb...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I frequently ask engineering candidates what the difference between a git rebase and a git merge is.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I have heard so many (100+) garbled, nonsensical, or subtly wrong answers -- but always using the right vocab -- over the past few months, that at this point I feel totally fried and would not personally answer this question as well as I would have before I started doing this.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: I frequently have to look it up just to override all the wrong stuff I am hearing.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: This is like context window pollution for LLMs!

dialogues.title: What have you been thinking about lately?

line-1.speaker: player
line-1.text: What have you been thinking about lately?

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: The following has been on my mind since I first encountered it almost 15 years ago.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: When I was in high school, I had a few teachers in the humanities/social sciences who were really, really good: deep, serious thinkers, with lots of interesting views synthesized over decades of globetrotting experiences.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: As teachers, even at a nice private school, they were not real "winners" in the sense of climbing a prestigious career ladder, and neither did they publish academic papers.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: You could call them very advanced amateurs, and as dabblers they got to toy with lots of interesting ideas, kind of randomly assembled, without outside judgment.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: When I got to the University of Chicago, known for its life of the mind in the humanities, I didn't really find anybody who seemed to be as deep or as interesting a thinker as these teachers I encountered in high school.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: Why do you think that is?

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Partially, it's because I got lucky with my teachers. They were the best we had. Maybe I didn't get so lucky with my professors.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: But today I may have figured it out: I think the actual reason is that my professors at UChicago were, in a sense, winners on an academic career ladder.

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: It's an extremely competitive environment, and they had somehow made it to the top. By definition, this is a tremendously powerful filter.

line-11.speaker: npc
line-11.text: And I think this had actually filtered against a whole group of people whom I consider interesting.

line-12.speaker: npc
line-12.text: This has become especially clear over the last few years, as a lot of traditional academia has been losing prestige rapidly: people are trusting the kind of professorial expert class less and less and less.

line-13.speaker: npc
line-13.text: It turned out that professors of ethics and sociology are just as unethical and susceptible to groupthink as the general public.

line-14.speaker: player
line-14.text: And the general conformity of ideology and thought in academia is now well-known.

line-15.speaker: npc
line-15.text: These professional humanities academics may publish papers that are respected or even highly esteemed within their own niche communities, but this particular value system has long since been removed from what I consider interesting, or, in many cases, even related to the pursuit of truth.

line-16.speaker: npc
line-16.text: Reflecting on it, the heart of the matter is that those teachers in high school were unconstrained by convention and had been allowed to fully lean into their interests --  kind of like the platonic dream of academia...

line-17.speaker: npc
line-17.text: Whereas the professors I encountered in university, even when very successful, had been conformed by the academia-industry pressure cooker and their work sanitized, professionalized, and ultimately made uninteresting under the constraints.

dialogues.title: Given the PyPI supply chain attack, I recommend keeping a canary in the coalm...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Given the PyPI supply chain attack, I recommend keeping a canary in the coalmine...

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I have a bitcoin private key containing $100 of BTC in my .bashrc. It's clearly labelled.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: If my system is ever compromised by some bad package, the BTC will get stolen, and I'll see the move on-chain. And that'll tell me that I need to rotate every single other secret.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: There are even services that will send you an alert (text, email, whatsapp...) if a given bitcoin address moves funds. It's good to have a burglar alarm, especially when time is of the essence.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: If you label it too obviously, won't a careful attacker just skip it on purpose to stay quiet longer?

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: Most attackers are not going to play that level of 3D chess, especially if the key has $100+ on it.

line-2.speaker: player

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: When American insurance juggernauts Ace-Westchester and Chubb merged, the surviving, now $100B+ public company, kept the worst of the three names.

dialogues.title: I am continuously surprised and impressed by the sheer number of things that ...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I am continuously surprised and impressed by the sheer number of things that Peter Thiel was and is right about, how early he was to them, and the courage with which he publicized them.

dialogues.title: There's an interesting pricing issue where the all-in cost of something is of...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: There's an interesting pricing issue where the all-in cost of something is often much more than the nominal cost of it, and so the nominal thing could actually be priced much higher, because the demand is so inelastic.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: For example. Say I pay $10 to go to an event, but I pay $20 for an Uber there, and $20 for an Uber back. My all-in cost is $50. They could've made the event 50% or 100% more expensive and it would've barely moved the needle.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: You would've easily paid.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Or suppose I'm going to a restaurant, but I'm taking a Waymo there vs. walking there. One of the two is $60 more expensive than the other, but it has no impact on the actual meal. If the restaurant knew, they could price that in.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: This reality is most revealed on DoorDash: the meal itself might cost only $20. But you're willing to pay another $15 to have it delivered. If you're willing to pay that, you're probably also willing to pay much more for the meal.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: This is why some DoorDash restaurants are absurdly expensive -- like $30 for a normal Indian curry -- because they've observed that the price of the dish doesn't really matter.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: Somehow the customer is already in a weird price-insensitive situation. They'll pay anything! They'll pay it on installments! (Really.)

line-8.speaker: player
line-8.text: This is a great insight and most consumer businesses don't grasp it well enough.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: I can't believe are clapping for "DoorDash is expensive because people will pay for it" and yet my multi-month gestation of "We seem to be on a billion-plus year old trend of increasing compute per second per unit matter" like a religious epiphany, gets crickets.

dialogues.title: I once was at a casual restaurant where I asked the waiter for ketchup.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I once was at a casual restaurant where I asked the waiter for ketchup.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: He said "Yeah we have ketchup" and then I watched him walk out, run across the street into a 7/11, and return with a handful of ketchup packets.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: Incredible.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: What's made the difference?

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: That's when the Waymos are cheap. I respond to financial incentives.

line-13.text: Carly Rae Jepsen's 2012 smash hit "Call Me Maybe" has always been suspicious to me.

line-14.speaker: npc
line-14.text: Already in 2012, people were no longer calling.

line-15.speaker: player
line-15.text: The texting generation was in full swing.

dialogues.title: Frozen peaches are a really good late-night snack.

line-17.text: Frozen peaches are a really good late-night snack.

line-18.speaker: npc
line-18.text: They satisfy in the same way as ice cream, but they're light on calories and healthy, and you naturally eat them slowly since they're frozen.

dialogues.title: Every now and again you run into some community that does not seem interested...

line-23.speaker: player

line-27.speaker: player

line-30.speaker: npc
line-30.text: That was the most pleasant voice.

line-33.speaker: npc

line-50.speaker: npc
line-50.text: I think the world is pretty fair in that you fundamentally get what you want.

line-53.speaker: npc

line-56.text: Nostalgia is big business. People pay through the nose for Disney experiences, rare Pokemon cards, you name it.

line-57.speaker: player

line-58.speaker: npc
line-58.text: It's a little sad, of course, to see people spend endlessly to try to relive memories or feelings that can never be felt again.

line-59.speaker: player
line-59.text: This suggests that people's preferences really get set fairly early in childhood, maybe around the teens, and then that's it for life.

line-60.speaker: npc
line-60.text: What that means is kind of interesting. The big businesses of the future will invest heavily to own the warm fuzzy feelings of childhood that will then create nostalgia-driven consumers for decades.

dialogues.title: Sometimes, an acquaintance will reach out to me to "catch up" casually. There...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Sometimes, an acquaintance will reach out to me to "catch up" casually. There's nothing I like more than a nice wide-ranging conversation with no agenda, so I usually say yes.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Then, 30 or 45 minutes in, they try to be very sneaky about this, they bring up -- oh-just-by-the-way -- some commercial request: an intro to so-and-so, maybe I'll consider buying their product, funding their company, whatever, and it's so disappointing...

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: The last half hour was a fake conversation, a plying motion to prepare for some sale, none of the personal interest was real.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: I understand that there's a certain school of thought in favor of doing this, but I don't like it at all.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: I much prefer when people reach out straightforwardly with their commercial request and none of the social fakery or time waste.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: I like doing the inversion: "Hey can you help with X?" and then afterwards ask to catch up.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: That's the way to do it.

dialogues.title: I can't stop thinking about the LA copper wire thefts.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I can't stop thinking about the LA copper wire thefts.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: For background: in LA, thieves have been stripping streetlights of their electrical wiring and selling it for scrap.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: It is amazingly destructive: for every $1 of wire they sell, the city has to spend $100-$1000 on repairs.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Literally, the thief might make a couple hundred bucks, and the city has to spend six figures.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Yes and the streetlights are out, which may lead to traffic accidents or other problems. It's an extremely antisocial crime.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: Astoundingly, the city seems unwilling to do something about this. A guy invented a better way to lock down streetlights -- they didn't want it. The idea of "look for the thieves and put them in jail" has been unpopular for reasons unclear to me.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: Proposed solutions, like making scrap yards record who sold them copper wiring, seem ineffective.

line-8.speaker: player
line-8.text: The most cynical explanation for this is that the incentives lead to crime.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: Right. The money spent on repairs is primarily spent on local union labor. For them, this is great. There's a whole industry for servicing these problems.

line-10.speaker: player
line-10.text: And the city gets to say that it is working on fixing the issues.

line-11.speaker: npc
line-11.text: Up to some limit, the more of these issues, the better.

line-12.speaker: npc
line-12.text: Everybody wins: the thieves win, the laborers win, the repair industry wins, certain politicians and candidates win. Well, the actual resident, the taxpayer -- they lose, but what are you gonna do?

line-13.speaker: player
line-13.text: Live with the lights off? Vote for the tough-on-crime candidate? Unthinkable.

line-14.speaker: npc
line-14.text: You can look at this as a system that has degenerated into being a recursive loop that drains the resources of its citizens.

line-52.text: Modern software founders are usually not really hackers.

line-53.speaker: player
line-53.text: We have way more hard-working, conventional high achievers now.

line-54.speaker: npc
line-54.text: The metaphor to the painter -- artist -- no longer holds very well. The founder archetype of Silicon Valley has been slowly changing.

line-55.speaker: player
line-55.text: Gone like the beer-on-tap and the ping-pong tables of 2015...

dialogues.title: Years ago, I spent some time studying the finance industry of the 70s and 80s...

line-57.speaker: npc
line-57.text: Years ago, I spent some time studying the finance industry of the 70s and 80s. Wild west days.

line-59.speaker: npc
line-59.text: Guys like Lou Ranieri literally worked their way up from the mail room -- they couldn't even get a job on wall street today.

line-60.speaker: player
line-60.text: I wondered then what it'd be like to show up as an unpolished hustler and get to pick all these low-hanging fruit.

line-61.speaker: npc
line-61.text: We're seeing it again today with AI.

dialogues.title: The microprocessor is the most complicated single thing we make.

line-63.speaker: npc
line-63.text: The microprocessor is the most complicated single thing we make.

line-64.speaker: npc
line-64.text: Knowing nothing else, you might expect we make very few of them -- but the real magic is that they're pretty much the most common objects on earth.

line-65.speaker: player
line-65.text: The most complicated thing is the most important thing and it is also the most abundant thing.

line-66.speaker: npc
line-66.text: Reminds a bit of Jevons paradox, it's a similar type of counter-intuition.

dialogues.title: Sometimes people discuss IQ numbers like 100, 70, 145, etc. But these are (li...

line-68.speaker: npc
line-68.text: Sometimes people discuss IQ numbers like 100, 70, 145, etc. But these are (literally!) just labels on a normal distribution: it'd be more useful to say "50th percentile" or "4 standard deviations out".

line-69.speaker: npc
line-69.text: It's a little weird that we wound up with this "IQ score" nomenclature -- most likely just because of a lack of statistical literacy?

line-70.speaker: player
line-70.text: A little ironic, don't you think?

dialogues.title: There are two types of video games: those with increasing difficulty, and tho...

line-72.speaker: npc
line-72.text: There are two types of video games: those with increasing difficulty, and those with constant difficulty, but more stuff, as you proceed.

line-73.speaker: npc
line-73.text: The former is played for achievement and fun, the latter is a numbing agent.

dialogues.title: I don't think anyone told me that one of the joys of childhood is never havin...

line-76.speaker: npc
line-76.text: I don't think anyone told me that one of the joys of childhood is never having to shave.

line-77.speaker: npc
line-77.text: Rosy smooth cheeks -- nobody ever said "Enjoy it while it lasts, one day you'll be permanently covered in stubble."

dialogues.title: Public markets and accredited investor laws interact in interesting ways.

line-79.speaker: npc
line-79.text: Public markets and accredited investor laws interact in interesting ways.

line-80.speaker: npc
line-80.text: Public markets were regulated to protect retail investors with laws on what financial data must be reported, what accounting standards are acceptable, and so on.

line-81.speaker: npc
line-81.text: This proved too onerous, so companies stayed private longer.

line-82.speaker: player
line-82.text: But retail investors still want access, so some people want to shred the accredited investor laws altogether.

line-83.speaker: npc
line-83.text: But that seems like the worst of both worlds: the opacity and pay-to-play of private markets, mixed with the lack of common standards and regulatory watchdogs of public markets.

line-84.speaker: player
line-84.text: I'm sure that retail would largely lose money, as they did in crypto.

line-85.speaker: npc
line-85.text: To resolve this tension, I think the right solution is to make it easy for private companies to go public earlier.

line-86.speaker: player
line-86.text: That's much better for the public and for the economy than removing accreditation laws.

dialogues.title: Exile is a punishment that no longer exists in our well-partitioned world.

line-88.speaker: npc
line-88.text: Exile is a punishment that no longer exists in our well-partitioned world.

line-89.speaker: npc
line-89.text: It was a very powerful concept because it conveys "we don't want to kill you, but you cannot impose costs on us any longer".

line-90.speaker: player
line-90.text: It's interesting because there are a lot of people today in that position, but we have no adequate legal/judicial response.

dialogues.title: One thing that's weird about your 30s is that you'll see some people, whom yo...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: One thing that's weird about your 30s is that you'll see some people, whom you know well personally, whom you saw as very smart and very successful, totally go off the rails.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Lose their minds, become radicalized, et cetera.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: Just staying sane is underrated as an objective.

dialogues.title: I just realized that 2022-2027 is probably the first time that more silicon v...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I just realized that 2022-2027 is probably the first time that more silicon valley technologists become UHNW wealthy as employees than as founders.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: The standard advice was to get a nice tech job.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Contrarian advice was to start a company.

line-4.speaker: player
line-4.text: Contrarian contrarian advice was to get a nice tech job... And pick correctly.

dialogues.title: My Gen-Z wife asked me, What if we get too many coins? Can we put them back i...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: My Gen-Z wife asked me, What if we get too many coins? Can we put them back in our account somehow?

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: And I told her yes. We can deposit them at the bank. When I was a child, I would carry my Deutschmarks to the bank, in a little satchel. The clerk would print my new balance in a booklet.

dialogues.title: Coffee shops will play music. Bars will sometimes play sports games, or even ...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Coffee shops will play music. Bars will sometimes play sports games, or even TV or movies.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: But I've never been to any establishment that plays a podcast.

dialogues.title: The 2005-onwards "fuel efficiency" era of cars has resulted in incredibly ugl...

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: The 2005-onwards "fuel efficiency" era of cars has resulted in incredibly ugly vehicles.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: Regulatory standards and pressure for aerodynamics have turned everything on four wheels into giant bloblike hatchbacks.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: Take a good look at one of these things. Horrendous.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: Once we get electric power + EVs at scale, we can go back to having vehicles that look good.

dialogues.title: I often think of J Robert Oppenheimer's retreat to St John's in the US Virgin...

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: I often think of J Robert Oppenheimer's retreat to St John's in the US Virgin Islands in the 1950s.

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: Imagine you're the most important nuclear physicist on earth, you've gone through staggering political drama, and then you peace out to a little pre-industrial island with no telephone or radio and sit on the beach for a couple weeks or months at a time.

dialogues.title: I saw an old clip of the Simpsons, where they visit a lawyer to execute a wil...

line-13.speaker: npc
line-13.text: I saw an old clip of the Simpsons, where they visit a lawyer to execute a will. It's in-person in an office.

line-14.speaker: npc
line-14.text: Sign of the times, today this would be done over Zoom and DocuSign.

line-15.speaker: player
line-15.text: The more valuable the profession by the hour, the more it is done virtually!

line-16.speaker: npc
line-16.text: Modern media struggles to capture a world in which your entire life happens on a screen.

dialogues.title: It would be good for everyone to spend a few days working in construction, ti...

line-18.speaker: npc
line-18.text: It would be good for everyone to spend a few days working in construction, tilling a field, cleaning streets, or manufacturing garments to appreciate (1) what goes on in our economy and (2) the benefits of modern technology.

line-19.speaker: player
line-19.text: People do not know how good they have it.

line-20.speaker: npc
line-20.text: There are a lot of anti-capitalists romanticizing pre-industrial life. People need to be inoculated against these illusions.

line-21.speaker: player
line-21.text: The biggest item is to spend a week washing clothes by hand: you will never look at a washing machine the same way again.

dialogues.title: Many places are named after some heritage (e.g. New York), a landmark, or a p...

line-23.speaker: npc
line-23.text: Many places are named after some heritage (e.g. New York), a landmark, or a person. But a lot of places are just named after money.

line-24.speaker: npc
line-24.text: It's uncommon in English, but if you start translating, it's everywhere: Puerto Rico? Rich Port!

dialogues.title: I suspect that a lot of AI applications are already subtly Infinite Jest mach...

line-27.speaker: npc
line-27.text: I suspect that a lot of AI applications are already subtly Infinite Jest machines, encouraging the user to use them more and more, hooking them on the *feeling of productivity* more so than on actual productivity.

line-28.speaker: npc
line-28.text: There's a big bill and rude awakening coming to some of these users. If you didn't like social media because it maximizes engagement, you've seen nothing yet.

line-29.speaker: player
line-29.text: The true engagement-maximizer, vastly smarter than you, billed by the token, is just in its infancy now.

dialogues.title: Nice hotels are like real-life Pinterest boards. At some point you're not pay...

line-31.speaker: npc
line-31.text: Nice hotels are like real-life Pinterest boards. At some point you're not paying for amenities but for curation and inspiration.

line-32.speaker: player
line-32.text: Like paying an interior designer for a few hours to sample a fully executed vision for a feeling of living.

dialogues.title: Reviews for nice hotels are funny because people are so religious about them.

line-34.speaker: npc
line-34.text: Reviews for nice hotels are funny because people are so religious about them.

line-35.speaker: npc
line-35.text: I was recently picking between Hotel A and B, and looking at the reviews on Reddit: half of them are "A sucks, B is the only way to go" and the other half is the exact opposite.

line-36.speaker: npc
line-36.text: As far as I can tell, these hotels are basically the same.

line-37.speaker: player
line-37.text: The tyranny of small differences is everywhere!

dialogues.title: Cookie popups are so dumb. This is a real policy-meets-technology failure.

line-39.speaker: npc
line-39.text: Cookie popups are so dumb. This is a real policy-meets-technology failure.

line-40.speaker: player
line-40.text: Your cookie settings should be sent as a default browser header.

line-41.speaker: npc
line-41.text: But maybe that didn't get implemented because it'd make it too easy to reject them all.

dialogues.title: I've tried reading the Odyssey a few times. I've always struggled with classi...

line-44.speaker: npc
line-44.text: I've tried reading the Odyssey a few times. I've always struggled with classical verse, I lose concentration too easily with it.

line-45.speaker: npc
line-45.text: I'm now listening to the Odyssey as an audiobook, and it's working a lot better.

line-46.speaker: player
line-46.text: Perhaps unsurprisingly: the old epics are meant to be read aloud!

dialogues.title: There's nothing more annoying than motorized trunk hatches on cars.

line-48.speaker: npc
line-48.text: There's nothing more annoying than motorized trunk hatches on cars.

line-49.speaker: npc
line-49.text: I want to throw in my bags and shut the trunk -- and so I put my hand on the license plate, and push -- it resists, starts beeping, and then the world's slowest motor begins whirring, it opens back up, I have to click some dumb small button with a hatch/door icon on it, and then it begins closing with a speed of maybe one inch per second.

line-51.speaker: npc
line-51.text: I have to stand there, waiting to make sure the damn thing is closing, feeling the seconds of my life leave my body.

dialogues.title: It is continuously amusing to me that the Bush family consists of the biggest...

line-53.speaker: npc
line-53.text: It is continuously amusing to me that the Bush family consists of the biggest WASPs there ever were, truly New Englanders incarnate, and then they decided to remake themselves as humble Texans.

dialogues.title: Looking back, it's interesting how "thin" the machine learning skill tree is ...

line-55.speaker: npc
line-55.text: Looking back, it's interesting how "thin" the machine learning skill tree is now. LSTMs, Random Forests, SVMs, etc. etc. have turned out to be ~irrelevant.

line-56.speaker: npc
line-56.text: Depth along one particularly powerful set of techniques beats all breadth.

line-57.speaker: player
line-57.text: Yep! There are a few remarkable things about rapidly climbing the exponential curve, one of them is that the playing field resets with some regularity.

dialogues.title: History is a strong quality filter for media: Herodotus, Chaucer, Shakespeare...

line-59.speaker: npc
line-59.text: History is a strong quality filter for media: Herodotus, Chaucer, Shakespeare, etc. were the best of their time, most other stuff simply didn't survive because it had to be manually replicated, and that's a high bar.

line-60.speaker: npc
line-60.text: Now we have a non-stop explosion of new cultural artifacts, not just due to AI, but internet-era connectedness in the first place.

line-61.speaker: player
line-61.text: I wonder if (1) it's possible to measure the outputs on a relative scale, e.g. every year we produce more cultural media than we have remaining from 2000BC to 1900AD combined, and...

line-62.speaker: player
line-62.text: (2) If there's a similar filter in the modern day -- like, there's so much ephemeral output that the act of reviewing, recommending, or replicating something carries a huge amount of weight.

dialogues.title: If you're sending an email to ask someone for something, the probability of g...

line-64.speaker: npc
line-64.text: If you're sending an email to ask someone for something, the probability of getting a reply is far-and-away maximized if you only ask for one thing as clearly as possible.

dialogues.title: I keep a lot of notes on things to write about, but it feels like many of the...

line-66.speaker: npc
line-66.text: I keep a lot of notes on things to write about, but it feels like many of them are rapidly becoming irrelevant under changes due to AI.

line-67.speaker: player
line-67.text: Just as parents often raise their children for the prior generation, writers publish for a world that has already disappeared.

line-68.speaker: npc
line-68.text: It takes great discipline to write for the present or the future.

dialogues.title: It appears that PPT slideshows and PDF decks are going away, in favor of AI-g...

line-70.speaker: npc
line-70.text: It appears that PPT slideshows and PDF decks are going away, in favor of AI-generated HTML websites.

line-71.speaker: player
line-71.text: Just as good to present, and way more flexible.

line-72.speaker: npc
line-72.text: It's interesting how AI means more centralization on the most common standards.

dialogues.title: What exactly is "affordable healthcare"? What standard of care are we really ...

line-74.speaker: npc
line-74.text: What exactly is "affordable healthcare"? What standard of care are we really talking about?

line-75.speaker: player
line-75.text: All the politics and debate, and I'm not sure if people even agree on a definition here.

dialogues.title: The great challenge with dentistry is that any operation removes all evidence...

line-77.speaker: npc
line-77.text: The great challenge with dentistry is that any operation removes all evidence that the procedure was necessary.

line-78.speaker: player
line-78.text: You can see how this creates misaligned incentives.

dialogues.title: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between history and fiction. In many ...

line-80.speaker: npc
line-80.text: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between history and fiction. In many cases, our understanding of past events is probably way off.

line-82.speaker: npc
line-82.text: Being able to tell a grand narrative of humanity is important to our sense of identity and philosophical self-actualization, but to what extent is truth important to that narrative?

line-83.speaker: player
line-83.text: It matters if we want to use the narrative to understand ourselves today.

line-84.speaker: npc
line-84.text: But beyond that, I want to say that there is intrinsic value in truth, but I struggle to make a really persuasive case to myself.

dialogues.title: David Foster Wallace writing Infinite Jest in response to (fundamentally) cab...

line-86.speaker: npc
line-86.text: David Foster Wallace writing Infinite Jest in response to (fundamentally) cable television of the '80s and '90s -- stuff that we would consider simply dull today -- is just incredible. To him this was already a colossally overwhelming force of entertainment, shaking the very foundations of what it means to be a human being.

line-87.speaker: player
line-87.text: If he could see what we have today...

dialogues.title: Under Donald Trump's second term, the concept of a "First Lady" has almost en...

line-89.speaker: npc
line-89.text: Under Donald Trump's second term, the concept of a "First Lady" has almost entirely disappeared.

dialogues.title: I think that Bitcoin and LLMs feel like they were switched in the order in wh...

line-91.speaker: npc
line-91.text: I think that Bitcoin and LLMs feel like they were switched in the order in which they should have arisen.

line-92.speaker: npc
line-92.text: AI provides abundance, eliminating scarcity. What's scarce, and thereby valuable, in that AI era? Well, Bitcoin provides one thing: provable scarcity.

line-93.speaker: player
line-93.text: Perhaps it arriving fifteen-plus years before its time and then languishing is like the 2010s all over again.

line-94.speaker: npc
line-94.text: Right. There may come to be a rhyme to this history. And consider how many of the problems surfaced by AI -- authenticity, provenance, et cetera -- are solved by crypto, by having some personal private key and the ability to stake money on a statement.

line-95.speaker: player
line-95.text: It felt like the crypto wave of the 2020s was a set of solutions in search of problems, and now we're finally getting those problems.

line-96.speaker: npc
line-96.text: It really feels like the timeline was inverted here.

dialogues.title: Sometimes I think about the 100 Prisoners Problem. This really blew my mind w...

line-98.speaker: npc
line-98.text: Sometimes I think about the 100 Prisoners Problem. This really blew my mind when I encountered it over a decade ago: it feels magical that there can be mathematical order like this in the world, that you wouldn't see at all unless you have the training.

line-99.speaker: player
line-99.text: Like a secret hidden in plain sight.

dialogues.title: Honor Codes That Work always feel remarkable to me, like a pinnacle of civili...

line-101.speaker: npc
line-101.text: Honor Codes That Work always feel remarkable to me, like a pinnacle of civilization.

line-102.speaker: player
line-102.text: There is great comfort in being able to trust the honesty of others, that people will do what they say they're going to do.

line-103.speaker: npc
line-103.text: This may be a big part of our story: humans have been successful in part because they bias toward cooperation, even when defecting might be more rational.

line-104.speaker: player
line-104.text: Conversely, I feel great unease when I see these honor/trust-systems weakened, and I suspect there is much more loss there than appears at first glance.

dialogues.title: I am continuously surprised that restaurants don't copy each other better. Fo...

line-106.speaker: npc
line-106.text: I am continuously surprised that restaurants don't copy each other better. For example, why do cafes serve bad sandwiches?

line-107.speaker: player
line-107.text: It's easy to learn how to make a good sandwich!

line-108.speaker: npc
line-108.text: And ingredients are obviously a readily available commodity.

dialogues.title: As a child, my mother would tell me the classic German saying "If you have ne...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: As a child, my mother would tell me the classic German saying "If you have never eaten cake in bed, you do not know how much crumbs poke you."

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: This was always presented to me as literal advice about not eating snacks in bed, but it has finally dawned on me that this is a metaphor.

dialogues.title: Let me tell you about my morning in San Francisco.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Let me tell you about my morning in San Francisco.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: I wake up. Normally I take a Waymo downtown, but today I walk over to Golden Gate Park.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: Early in the morning, before 8:00, the park is bathed in a heavy fog. The mist hangs in the air and you can feel it on your cheeks as you walk.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: The park is hilly and thick with green of the grass and the trees. The birds chirp from far out of sight. In that moment, the world feels still. The dew will leave your sneakers wet if you walk across the meadows. Backpack on, walking up a slight incline in the grey and green, feels like you might be climbing up a misty mountain top somewhere far away.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: I walk all the way through the park to its very south-eastern corner, and keep walking east through Cole Valley.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: The fog quickly ends there, from one block to the next, and some of the most picturesque Victorians in the city have their colors revealed by the soft sunlight. In the center of Cole Valley is a cafe called Wooden Coffeehouse that has the most comfortable, finely curved handmade wooden chairs in the city.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: I purchase a cappuccino, which is rich and creamy, and I think about how much I love being there.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Across the street is a streetcar stop. It moves quickly and smoothly and carves its way straight through the hills in the center of the city.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: When it drops me off at my workplace among all the high-rises downtown, there's not a drop of fog in the air, just the pure great sun of California that I had been told about and imagined long before I first arrived here.

dialogues.title: (1) Akira and (2) Infinite Jest are similar in how it feels like the author w...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: (1) Akira and (2) Infinite Jest are similar in how it feels like the author wanted to write a cool story about (1) motorcycles/sci-fi Tokyo and (2) tennis/drugs, but just couldn't resist the call of (1) supernatural nuclear armageddon and (2) people's relationship to entertainment.

dialogues.title: Oh by the way.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Oh by the way.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: Yes?

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: If you believe in a "permanent underclass", it should be obvious that there will be no overclass.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: In the face of an arbitrarily expanding power differential, you being an "owner" of Class B Common Stock in The Last Company will be short-lived, and in retrospect, naive.

dialogues.title: I've been thinking a lot about AI disintermediating human relationships. This...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I've been thinking a lot about AI disintermediating human relationships. This seems like a real challenge to me, and I'm not sure how to feel about it.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Thanks to AI, in the long run there will be no need for me to ask anyone else for help with anything, and consequently, there will be no opportunity for people to feel useful and appreciated when they provide a service.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: That give-and-take between people is the core of our social fabric.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: And it has already been fraying for a long time, even pre-AI.

line-5.speaker: player
line-5.text: Many optimists say things like "AI will automate all the rote work so people can focus on their passions and being together" -- but there is no "being together" without some shared struggle or objective.

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: There is no building trust without need -- and in an AI-induced age of abundance, there may just not be any need.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: Social fabric is woven by countless daily small, necessary interactions with other people -- and those interactions may simply go away because your AI agent of choice ends up being your interface to the world around yourself.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Not because of any shortcoming, like being lazy or complacent, but because AI will be a better interface.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: Why ask your friend for advice when AI will be more patient, less judgmental, and understand you better? What's left for parents to teach their children if AI is a better tutor in all respects? And so forth.

line-10.speaker: player
line-10.text: Many incipient changes or risks due to AI do not worry me much. I am very optimistic about what AI can bring to our future. But this one challenge bothers me; it seems like it could spell a fundamental reorganization of our society, isolating the individual much more greatly than ever before.

line-11.speaker: npc
line-11.text: The consequences of this are not clear to me, but it doesn't look great -- generally, it seems that "isolating the individual" has not been good for either those individuals or their societies. And I don't think enough time or thought is being spent on what we want our social lives post-AGI to look like.

dialogues.title: There is a technical interview problem I like to ask which is so good, so cou...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: There is a technical interview problem I like to ask which is so good, so counter-intuitive, the key insight so delightful, that one of my employees is bringing her husband to the office today just to try the problem.

line-2.speaker: player
line-2.text: Is he interviewing with you?

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: No! First time for everything.

dialogues.title: "Coming of age" books or movies used to be about turning 16 or 18.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: "Coming of age" books or movies used to be about turning 16 or 18.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Now they're about turning 30.

line-3.speaker: player
line-3.text: Someone once said that life starts at 40 and everything else is research.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: I'm pretty sure the number in that saying used to be 30.

dialogues.title: I'm noticing the growing possibility that Europe becomes very poor in the cou...

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: I'm noticing the growing possibility that Europe becomes very poor in the course of the next 10-20 years. You have the following factors:

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: 1. Heavy industry totally uncompetitive against China, automakers etc. rapidly losing ground.

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: 2. Services industry totally uncompetitive against AI.

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: 3. No natural resources, or regulatory hurdles making their extraction impossible.

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: 4. No access to the new economy (no AI, no data centers, uncompetitive energy sector).

line-6.speaker: npc
line-6.text: 5. Client states caught in one-way welfare ratchets, spend reallocation + investment well-nigh impossible.

line-7.speaker: player
line-7.text: This seems under-contemplated.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: And we're talking really, seriously dirt poor: taken to its logical conclusion, many countries will have much, much smaller services and manufacturing industries -- economies may become much more heavily skewed toward natural resources and energy markets, where Europe has made it impossible for itself to compete.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: And I'm not saying that this is likely to happen, it's an extreme case. But the probability is greater than zero and appears to be growing.

line-10.speaker: npc
line-10.text: The EV of that is so negative that it's surprising to me that it's not coming up more.

line-11.speaker: player
line-11.text: But what about tourism? Like, consider the Mediterranean waterfront as a natural resource.

line-12.speaker: npc
line-12.text: Arguably the nicest Mediterranean weather in the world is in Cape Town, but South Africa is so far gone that they can no longer make productive use of it.

dialogues.title: Let me tell you about renovations. Never start.

line-1.speaker: npc
line-1.text: Let me tell you about renovations. Never start.

line-2.speaker: npc
line-2.text: Some people go crazy renovating their homes. After having done this for a few months, I understand why:

line-3.speaker: npc
line-3.text: First of all, it trains you to be hyperaware of errors. Your contractors are inevitably going to try to cut corners, and you want to both get your fair money's worth and have your vision executed, so you have to really pay attention, to things that normally you never would...

line-4.speaker: npc
line-4.text: Was that scratch there before? Is this cabinet level?

line-5.speaker: npc
line-5.text: Of course, once you're trained in this way, your hypervigilance extends to everything, even far outside your contractors' work: there's a half-inch gap between the doorframe and the floor? Sacrilege! Doesn't matter if it's been there for 40 years.

line-6.speaker: player
line-6.text: A home is a complex thing with lots of detail, so inevitably, no matter where you look, the flaws will be endless.

line-7.speaker: npc
line-7.text: Secondly, the other thing you learn is that whatever problems you see, you can fix them! Don't like it? Tear it out and do it again. If renting, you treat things as fixed -- but a house turns out to be shockingly malleable.

line-8.speaker: npc
line-8.text: Literally everything can be changed. You can move lights, pipes, doors, tear out walls, there are no limits.

line-9.speaker: npc
line-9.text: These are the two core learnings of doing renovations, and combined, they are very dangerous: for people who are not used to saying "good enough, whatever", this becomes an endless perfectionist loop.

line-10.speaker: player
line-10.text: I see. They'll have you changing stuff forever until you either run out of money or sanity.

line-11.speaker: npc
line-11.text: Worse, you'll find that changing one thing often implies changing another thing...

line-12.speaker: npc
line-12.text: I have a painting that looks like it's not level even though it is. Why? It's not aligned with the doorframe. Why? The doorframe itself isn't level. Why? The floor itself isn't level because it's 100 years old. But you can't live there while you're redoing the floors, of course.

line-13.speaker: player
line-13.text: This is a scope-creep, yak-shaving classic: all you wanted was to hang your painting straight and now you live in a storage unit. Beware.

dialogues.title: The croissant alibi

start.speaker: npc
start.text: Look at this bakery queue. Doesn't anyone work anymore? Yes, I'm in the queue. Yes, it is a weekday. How shall I explain myself?

choices.text: You are allowed to take a break.

a.speaker: npc
a.text: Excellent. A classic. What if my manager joins the queue?

choices.text: Ask what their computer is compiling.

a1.speaker: npc
a1.text: An unexpected peer review. We'll conduct it over pastry.

a2.speaker: npc
a2.text: A practical pivot from suspicious absence to valued team member.

b.speaker: npc
b.text: A dangerously humane explanation. What would make this a proper break?

b1.speaker: npc
b1.text: All right. I'll give my full professional attention to the croissant.

b2.speaker: npc
b2.text: Then hello. We've apparently been promoted from two people waiting to a conversation.

leave.speaker: npc
leave.text: May your pastry justify absolutely none of your life choices. It can just be good.
